abstract: Exosomes are an evolved sub-type of extracellular vesicles (EVs) that have gained popularity in recent years as a novel biological nanocarrier system for targeted precision therapy in cancer owing to their excellent biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, and high stability. While other artificial systems can only deliver specific types of drug, exosomes have been found to effectively carry different types of therapeutic cargo, such as chemotherapeutic agents, proteins, peptides, mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, and even CRISPR/Cas gene editing elements. Recent progress in exosome engineering technologies, such as surface modification, donor cell modification, bionic hybrid vesicles, and stimuli-responsive exosomes, has improved their targeting efficacy, cargo-loading capacity, and controlled drug release properties. Apart from their therapeutic use, exosomes play an active role in promoting tumor development by regulating the tumor microenvironment, angiogenesis, metastasis, immune escape, maintenance of cancer stem cells, and drug resistance. This review provides a brief insight into the biological properties of exosomes, recent developments in isolation and characterization methods, engineering approaches, therapeutic cargo loading, and their uses in targeted chemotherapy, gene and RNA therapy, immunotherapy, phototherapy, sonodynamic therapy, chemo-dynamic therapy, and combinational therapy. Moreover, the existing issues in exosome research, such as exosome heterogeneity, large-scale production, quality control, and regulatory issues, are addressed. Finally, new approaches involving artificial intelligence, multi-omics technology, and personalized engineering of exosomes are presented as potential solutions to enhance the clinical use of exosomes.

abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are among the most aggressive paediatric brain tumours, with the pathognomonic H3K27M mutation present in over 80% of cases. This mutation drives epigenetic dysregulation and transcriptional reprogramming, yet its impact on the tumour antigenic landscape remains poorly understood. Given the low mutational burden of DMG, an expanded search beyond neoantigens to include epigenetically dysregulated tumour-associated antigens (TAAs) is critical for advancing antigen-specific immunotherapies.
METHODS: We performed immunopeptidomic analysis of two patient-derived H3K27M-mutant DMG cell lines (SU-DIPG13 and BT245) and their isogenic counterparts in which only the mutant H3F3A allele was disrupted by CRISPR editing (H3K27M-KO), leaving wild-type histone H3.3 intact. High-resolution mass spectrometry and bioinformatics were used to define H3K27M-associated changes in the immunopeptidome, and functional T cell assays with HLA-matched healthy donor PBMCs assessed peptide immunogenicity.
RESULTS: H3K27M modulated the tumour antigenic landscape in a model-specific manner. Loss of the mutant allele increased HLA-I expression in SU-DIPG13 but not BT245, while immunopeptidomic profiling revealed distinct shifts in tumour-associated peptide presentation in both models, indicating that HLA-I abundance alone does not explain these changes. We identified six peptides derived from SLITRK2, PRAME, XKR5 and CBX2 that elicited T-cell responses in vitro; T cells raised against five of these preferentially recognised the parental H3K27M-mutant DMG cells. Several prioritised peptides were detected only in parental H3K27M-mutant cells, supporting mutation-associated, antigen-selective differences in peptide presentation and tumour antigenicity.
CONCLUSIONS: This study shows that H3K27M modulates the antigenic landscape in DMG in a model-dependent, antigen-selective manner, uncovering immunogenic tumour-associated peptides that could serve as targets for precision immunotherapy and establishing a foundation for T cell-based therapies in this otherwise treatment-refractory disease.

title: H3K27M Mutation Modulates the Antigenic Landscape in Diffuse Midline Glioma.

abstract: Current variant classifications do not capture clinical severity relative to other pathogenic variants in the same gene. We propose phenotype-exceeding-(mono)allelic-knockout (PEAK) as a term for variants associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than that of heterozygous null alleles. This mechanism-independent designation may facilitate genotype-phenotype interpretation and identify candidates for allele-selective therapeutic development.

title: PEAK: a phenotype-based classification of genetic variants.

abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder in which genetic susceptibility, aging, protein aggregation, and neuroglial dysfunction converge to drive progressive neuronal loss. Although animal models and conventional cell systems have provided fundamental insights into pathomechanisms, they only partially reproduce the human-specific and multifactorial nature of AD. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-based models have emerged as a powerful platform to investigate disease-relevant processes within a patient-specific genetic background while enabling the generation of multiple neural cell types and multicellular systems. In this review, we present the evolution of hiPSC-based AD modeling, from reductionist paradigms based on exogenous amyloid-β exposure to CRISPR-engineered isogenic models addressing causal mutations and genetic risk variants associated with either familial or sporadic forms. We examine the contribution of three-dimensional brain organoids and neuroglial co-culture systems in recapitulating cell-cell interactions, neuroinflammatory responses, and tissue-level pathological processes. We focus on current challenges, including the limited representation of neuronal aging, variability among organoids, and the need for standardized protocols. Finally, we discuss the translational potential of hiPSC-derived systems for target identification, drug discovery, and regenerative medicine. Collectively, these advances position hiPSC-based platforms as essential complementary models for elucidating AD pathogenesis and accelerating the development of precision therapeutic strategies.

title: From Amyloid Exposure to Genetic Causality: Converging hiPSC-Based Models of Alzheimer's Disease.

abstract: Glioblastoma, isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-wildtype (GBM), remains one of the most aggressive primary brain tumors, and its proteostasis machinery represents a potential therapeutic target. Here we identify HSP27 as a key regulator-associated proteostasis in glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, where it is linked to protein synthesis, folding, stress-granule dynamics and ubiquitin-mediated turnover. Ribo-seq showed HSP27 depletion reduced global protein synthesis, while TME labeling coupled to mass spectrometry revealed increased accumulation of unfolded proteins, indicating proteotoxic stress. Proteomic analysis of isolated stress granules (SGs) revealed enhanced sequestration of translational regulators, including EIF4E, mTOR, EIF3M and QKI, into stress granules (SGs), thereby reinforcing translational repression. Ubiquitinome profiling further revealed increased ubiquitination and proteasome-dependent loss of oncogenic and translational regulators, including AKT2, PARP1, EIF4G1, EIF4A3, and DDX5. Functionally, targeting HSP27 inhibits tumor growth and sensitizes glioblastoma to translational blockade. In orthotopic models, antisense oligonucleotide targeting HSP27 in combination with Didemnin B suppressed tumor progression and prolonged survival compared with either single agent. These findings associate HSP27 with proteostasis in glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, and suggest HSP27-dependent proteostasis buffering as a therapeutic vulnerability.

title: HSP27 Provides Stress-Adaptive Proteostasis Buffering in Glioblastoma and Is Therapeutically Vulnerable.

abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most lethal and intractable central nervous system malignancies, characterized by aggressive cellular proliferation, profound hypoxia, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. The primary pharmacokinetic obstacle for systemic interventions is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which restricts the infiltration of free therapeutic agents. To overcome this limitation, translational nanomedicine has driven the design of next-generation delivery systems, including liposomal vectors and synthetic organic, inorganic, and hybrid nanoparticles. This study establishes an exhaustive analysis of molecular targeting strategies designed to actively hijack physiological transport pathways via receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) targeting transferrin, lactoferrin, and LRP1 receptors and adsorption-mediated transcytosis (AMT) using polycationic biomaterials. Terminal selectivity via tumor-specific antigens, such as EGFRvIII and nucleolin (targeted by the AS1411 aptamer), is also discussed alongside smart stimuli-responsive platforms that exploit the tumor microenvironment's acidic pH, hypoxia, and matrix metalloproteinase activity for localized drug release. Concurrently, the deployment of these nanoplatforms for the intracellular vectorization of advanced genetic material, including siRNA (targeting VEGF and MGMT) and CRISPR/Cas9 complexes, demonstrates significant efficacy in reversing genomic chemoresistance and collapsing tumor neoangiogenesis. Finally, the review addresses critical bioengineering and clinical bottlenecks such as manufacturing scale-up, human BBB complexity, opsonization, and the long-term toxicity of inorganic nanoparticles that currently limit the regulatory transition of these highly promising neuro-oncological nanotechnologies from bench to bedside.

title: Next-Generation Liposomal and Nanoparticle-Based Systems for Glioblastoma: Molecular Targeting Strategies to Overcome the Blood-Brain Barrier.

abstract: Gene therapy offers a fundamental approach to treating genetic disorders, malignant tumors, and refractory chronic diseases by directly modifying or replacing defective genes at the molecular level. Driven by policy support, increased investment, and technological innovation, China has achieved remarkable progress in adenoviral and adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, gene editing, genetically engineered immune cells, oncolytic microorganisms, and small nucleic acid drugs. This review provides a comprehensive narrative overview of the technical principles, product pipelines, and clinical advances in these fields. Notable achievements include the approval of AAV-based gene therapy products in China, the entry of multiple in vivo and ex vivo gene editing therapies into clinical trials, a leading number of CAR-T trials worldwide with expansion into solid tumors and autoimmune diseases, encouraging efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy in liver cancer and melanoma, and positive clinical data of small interfering RNA/antisense oligonucleotide drugs for chronic hepatitis B and hypercholesterolemia. However, challenges remain including suboptimal tissue specificity, off-target risks, limited cargo capacity, high production costs, and poor accessibility. Future directions should focus on tissue-selective vectors, precise editing tools, off-the-shelf cell products, scalable manufacturing, and improved regulatory frameworks. With abundant clinical resources and strong manufacturing capabilities, China is poised to play a significant role in the global gene therapy landscape.

title: Novel Technologies and Clinical Breakthroughs: The Evolving Landscape of Gene Therapy in China.

abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of severe lower respiratory tract disease in infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals, underscoring the need for vaccine strategies that balance systemic protection with frontline respiratory immunity. Although adenoviral and RNA-based RSV are both promising platforms, how the platform itself shapes systemic versus respiratory mucosal immunity under the same antigenic context remains insufficiently defined. We conducted a head-to-head comparison of an LNP-delivered saRNA vaccine (LNP-RSV-preF saRNA) and a recombinant Ad5-vectored vaccine (Ad5-RSV-preF) in mice using intramuscular prime-boost immunization. The two platforms drove distinct immune architectures rather than just differences in response magnitude. LNP-RSV-preF saRNA preferentially promoted respiratory mucosal immunity, including elevated BALF IgG, pulmonary antibody-secreting cells, CD69+ T cells, and lung-resident memory T (TRM) cells, as well as cycling and memory-associated CD8+ T-cell states and durable lung IgA memory. In contrast, Ad5-RSV-preF induced stronger systemic immunity, featured by higher early serum IgG, splenic polyfunctional effector T cells, enhanced germinal center/TFH responses, and effector-polarized CD8 + T cells, with sustained systemic humoral memory. Ad5-vectored and LNP-saRNA vaccine platforms induce distinct compartmentalized immune responses to the same RSV preF antigen. This study establishes a framework for rational platform selection in RSV vaccine design, enabling tailored strategies to balance systemic immunity and respiratory mucosal memory.

abstract:
CAD is driven by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and is a major cause of myocardial infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death. Despite contemporary secondary prevention including lipid lowering, revascularization when indicated, and antiplatelet therapy, participants with established CAD, particularly those post-ACS, remain at clinically meaningful residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events.

Intensifying antithrombotic therapy can reduce ischemic events but typically increases bleeding, as exemplified by the addition of low dose rivaroxaban to aspirin in stable atherosclerotic disease. This persistent efficacy-safety trade-off supports development of antithrombotic approaches that reduce pathological thrombosis while preserving hemostasis.

RBD1119 is a GalNAc-conjugated siRNA that targets factor XI mRNA in hepatocytes. The GalNAc moiety binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocyte surfaces, enabling receptor mediated endocytosis and preferential hepatic uptake. Once internalized, RBD1119 mediates cleavage of factor XI mRNA via the RNA interference pathway, reducing hepatic factor XI expression and lowering circulating factor XI levels.

This multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II trial will evaluate the PD, safety, and PK of subcutaneously administered RBD1119 in participants with stable coronary artery disease (CAD).

description:
CAD is caused by atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries and remains a leading cause of MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, and premature death, with substantial residual risk of recurrent atherothrombotic events even after standard secondary prevention. More intensive antithrombotic therapy can lower ischemic events, but this benefit is often offset by increased bleeding, highlighting the need for treatments that better separate antithrombotic efficacy from bleeding risk. Factor XI, part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway, has emerged as a promising target because its inhibition reduces thrombin amplification and prolongs aPTT without affecting prothrombin time, suggesting potential for safer anticoagulation with less disruption of normal hemostasis.

The trial comprises screening, treatment, and long-term safety follow-up periods. Participants will be allocated to one of three different dose levels of RBD1119 or placebo: low-dose (n=40), medium-dose (n=60), high-dose (n=60) or placebo (n=40). Approximately 200 participants will be randomized.

Randomization to the RBD1119 low-dose dose group and corresponding placebo proceeds without dose-specific staggering. Randomization to the medium-dose group is initially limited to 10 participants, comprising 8 participants assigned to RBD1119 medium-dose and 2 assigned to placebo. Further randomization is paused until participants have received Dose X on Day Y and completed safety follow-up through Day 43. Randomization resumes only after IDMC review, a recommendation to continue, and Sponsor authorization. Initiation of the high-dose group requires prior IDMC review of the initial medium-dose cohort and Sponsor authorization. The same initial cohort, safety follow-up, IDMC review, and authorization process is then applied to the high-dose group. A planned IDMC review will not be delayed solely because fewer than all 10 participants in an initial dose cohort have received the second dose or completed follow-up through Day 43.

abstract: Cells expressing monoallelic HLA class I molecules represent a convenient in vitro model for studying the immunogenicity of tumor protein neoepitopes. Such models can be generated using endogenous HLA class I-deficient cells. Here, we describe an effective method for eliminating HLA class I expression in HEK293T cells via simultaneous CRISPR/Cas9 editing of the HLA‑A, HLA‑B, and HLA‑C genes using a single guide RNA. An important advantage of this method is the possibility to maintain the unedited HLA‑E gene. The antigen-presenting function of the resulting cells was successfully restored by transduction of a single HLA class I allele. Cells expressing monoallelic HLA‑A, after processing SARS-CoV‑2 epitopes, induced the allele-specific immune response in leukocytes isolated from patients who had recovered from COVID-19. Thus, the obtained HLA class I-knockout cells can be used to evaluate allele-specific neoantigen presentation.

abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.

abstract: Salvia miltiorrhiza Bunge is a valuable medicinal plant, yet its genetic manipulation has been limited by the lack of efficient and practical transformation methods. Here, we report a simplified, tissue culture-independent strategy enabling Agrobacterium-mediated gene delivery under non-sterile conditions, termed hypocotyl acupuncture. The method employs needle-assisted inoculation of intact seedlings at the hypocotyl, completely bypassing callus induction, regeneration, and repeated subculture. Following inoculation, EGFP-positive hairy roots are selectively cultivated for approximately 4 months and then induced to regenerate shoots within one additional month, yielding transgenic plantlets in approximately 5 months. Systematic optimization achieved a transformation efficiency of approximately 55% (defined as the percentage of explants producing EGFP-positive regenerants). ACCC10060 was selected as the optimal strain based on efficiency and root morphology. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing generated mutation frequencies of 53.8%-88.9% with no off-target effects. Targeted mutagenesis of SmCPS1, a gene encoding a key rate-limiting enzyme in tanshinone biosynthesis, resulted in altered root pigmentation. The method was successfully extended to Astragalus membranaceus, Platycodon grandiflorus, and Isatis indigotica, achieving transformation efficiencies of 25%-55%. This study provides an efficient, practical, and broadly applicable tool for genome editing and functional genomics in medicinal plants.

abstract: Land plant mitochondria and plastids are endosymbiotic organelles that possess their own, reduced genomes. Gene expression is largely regulated at the transcript level, predominantly by nuclear-encoded proteins. Notably, up to thousands of cytidines in organellar RNAs are specifically edited to uridines, mostly restoring conserved genetic information. Key players in this process are nuclear-encoded pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, which bind target RNAs in a one-PPR:one-nucleotide manner, following a two-amino-acid-based code. Cytidine deamination is catalyzed by intrinsic or trans-acting DYW domains. The modularity and programmability of PPR-RNA interactions make PPR editing factors attractive candidates for the development of biotechnological tools. However, RNA target selection is not determined by the 'PPR code' alone, hampering the generation of highly effective and specific editors. Refining such tools requires efficient assays to dissect the determinants of editor-RNA interaction. Here, we introduce a rapid assay to assess PPR editor specificity through transient expression in the cytosol of Nicotiana benthamiana, which offers a large and diverse transcriptome that enables extensive off-target editing. Profiling of these off-targets provides comprehensive information on an editor's target selectivity. Compared with a previous setup in the model moss Physcomitrium patens, which relies on stable transformation, the required experimental time is reduced from months to days. We demonstrate the power of the system by characterizing the off-targets of the moss editor PpPPR56. The new assay allows rapid functional assessment of editing factor variants and removes a bottleneck in understanding editor-RNA interactions, which is a prerequisite for the rational improvement of PPR-based RNA editing tools.

abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) remains one of the most important staple crops worldwide and serves as a primary source of calories and protein for billions of people. Global wheat production, however, continues to be threatened by rust diseases caused by Puccinia triticina, Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici and Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. These pathogens are highly adaptive and frequently give rise to new virulent races, causing resistance in wheat cultivars to breakdown. Under favorable environmental conditions, severe epidemics can develop and substantial yield losses may occur. In response to these challenges, traditional management approaches such as resistant cultivars, crop rotation, sanitation and fungicide application have long been employed in wheat production systems. Yet these strategies have increasingly been constrained by resistance breakdown, genetic uniformity in modern cultivars, and climate-driven changes in pathogen distribution. Conventional management practices are evaluated alongside emerging technological solutions including genomic-assisted breeding, gene pyramiding, CRISPR-based genome editing, biological control agents and precision agriculture tools. In addition, nanotechnology has emerged as a promising tool in plant disease management, where nanoparticles such as silver, copper and zinc oxide exhibit strong antifungal activity and enable targeted delivery of agrochemicals. Nano-enabled formulations can enhance fungicide efficiency, reduce chemical inputs and improve plant defense responses, offering a sustainable complement to existing wheat rust management strategies. Particular attention is given to integrated disease management strategies, which combine traditional agronomic practices with modern surveillance technologies such as remote sensing, artificial intelligence-based forecasting models, and pathogen genomics. These combined approaches can improve resistance durability and build more resilient wheat production systems. Future directions emphasize climate adaptation, global surveillance and collaborative breeding. In an era of increasing climatic uncertainty and evolving pathogen populations, durable rust management will depend on coordinated global efforts that align scientific innovation, farmer adoption, and policy support to safeguard wheat productivity and global food security.

abstract: Dendrobium officinale is an important medicinal Orchidaceae species with considerable ecological and economic value. While its chloroplast genome has been well characterized, the structure features of its mitochondrial genome remain largely unexplored, which further hinders our understanding of its evolutionary dynamics and adaptive mechanisms. This study presents a comprehensive characterization of the mitochondrial genome of D. officinale, revealing a complex multibranched structure of 22 chromosomes totaling 639,931 bp, encoding 35 PCGs, 3 rRNA genes, and 24 tRNA genes. Codon usage analysis revealed a distinct codon bias, while the genome harbors abundant repetitive elements and 522 RNA editing sites. Comparative genomic analysis identified 125 MTPT fragments totaling 108,012 bp (16.88% of the mitogenome), indicating frequent inter-organellar DNA transfer. Dendrobium nobile exhibited the highest genomic homology with D. officinale. Ka/Ks analysis indicated that most mitochondrial genes are under strong purifying selection. In addition, we conducted a comparative analysis between the newly assembled mitochondrial genome of D. officinale and seven Orchidaceae species. Phylogenetic analysis based on the maximum likelihood, maximum parsimony and bayesian inference approaches resolved the phylogenetic position of D. officinale within Orchidaceae. Collectively, these findings provide a valuable reference for future studies on Orchidaceae phylogenomics and mitochondrial evolution.

abstract: Genome editing is becoming an important tool for crop improvement by enabling precise modification of genetic variation. CRISPR-Cas technologies have expanded beyond nuclease-induced mutations to include base and prime editing, transcriptional and epigenetic regulation, multiplex editing, organelle editing and targeted DNA insertion. These advances support the development of agronomically valuable alleles and extend crop improvement beyond conventional selection, recombination and random mutagenesis. Applications now include plant architecture, yield-related traits, resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses, seed composition and nutritional quality, and extend to de novo domestication, haploid induction and hybrid breeding. Current research is increasingly moving from single-gene modification toward the engineering of promoters, cis-regulatory elements, quantitative alleles and multiple-gene editing, particularly in polyploid crops. Wider breeding applications will depend on efficient delivery and regeneration, recovery of transgene-free and heritable edited germplasm, reliable targeted insertion and validation across relevant environments. Integration with pangenomics, multi-omics, phenomics, artificial intelligence and predictive breeding may further improve target identification, allele design and prediction of editing outcomes, thereby supporting the development of more precise and efficient crop-breeding strategies.

abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is one of the most prevalent degenerative joint diseases, and there is no approved pharmacological therapy that can reliably reverse cartilage degeneration or restore cartilage structure. Allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have shown therapeutic potential for OA, but inflammatory conditions can enhance HLA expression and increase allogeneic immune recognition risk. Here, we generated B2M and CIITA double-knockout induced pluripotent stem cells (dKO-iPSCs) using CRISPR/Cas9 and subsequently differentiated them into dKO-iMSCs. B2M/CIITA double-knockout did not affect iPSC pluripotency, karyotype, or teratoma formation. dKO-iMSCs retained characteristic MSC phenotypes, exhibited greater proliferative capacity than tissue-derived MSCs, and could be expanded to passage 18. Notably, HLA-ABC and HLA-DR expression remained undetectable in dKO-iMSCs even after IFN-γ stimulation. In co-culture assays with PHA-L-stimulated allogeneic PBMCs, dKO-iMSCs suppressed PBMC and T-cell proliferation as effectively as wild-type iMSCs, indicating preservation of their immunomodulatory activity. Intra-articular administration of dKO-iMSCs significantly reduced cartilage degeneration in the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model of OA. The treatment showed greater therapeutic efficacy than wild-type iMSCs and tissue-derived MSCs and did not cause evident systemic organ toxicity. Single-cell RNA sequencing of BM-MSCs and dKO-iMSCs after in vitro IFN-γ stimulation revealed enhanced extracellular matrix-associated cell-cell communication and markedly reduced IL1B expression in dKO-iMSCs, indicating a less pro-inflammatory and more matrix-supportive cellular state under inflammatory conditions. Collectively, B2M/CIITA double-knockout enables sustained reduction in HLA expression while preserving the MSC phenotype and immunomodulatory activity, and enhances the therapeutic efficacy of iMSCs in the mouse OA model, providing a potential strategy for developing iPSC-derived MSCs with reduced HLA expression for allogeneic cell therapy.

title: HLA-Engineered iPSC-Derived Mesenchymal Stromal Cells for the Treatment of Osteoarthritis in Mice.

abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.
